html:
Dutch Brazil was a colony of the Dutch Republic on the northeast coast of Brazil, held from 1630 to 1654. The map places the label near the mouth of the Amazon, where Dutch traders also had small posts early in the 1600s; the colony's centre was further east, at Recife.

The Dutch West India Company seized Recife and Olinda from Portugal in 1630 to take over the richest sugar region of the world. Under the governor Johan Maurits, from 1637 to 1644, the colony grew. He built the new town of Mauritsstad, brought painters such as Frans Post and scientists to record the land, and allowed freedom of worship. Recife's Jews built the Kahal Zur Israel synagogue, the first in the Americas.

In 1645 Portuguese planters rose in revolt, and they beat the Dutch twice at Guararapes in 1648 and 1649. Recife surrendered in 1654, and the land went back to Portuguese Brazil. Some Jews and planters moved on to the Caribbean and to New Amsterdam, taking sugar know-how with them.
